title: How do the fold lines and turns change along the snowflake shapes?
description: The last row of shapes in the table of Chapter one is the snowflake sequence, with five shapes that start from a triangle and grow smaller bumps. Folding and turning each one gives its lines and angles of symmetry. The video checks the idea that more bumps give more fold lines, and the later shapes keep the same six lines.
teaching_notes: One idea: bumps added in the same way on every side do not create new fold lines or new turns. Watch for students who think the count keeps growing with the number of bumps.

source: Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.2, second block)
video_script.why: The child counts the lines and the angles of symmetry of each of five snowflake shapes, and sees that after the second shape the counts stop changing.
video_script.substitution: Cut each snowflake shape from paper, fold it every way the halves match, then pin it at the centre and turn it.
video_script.anchor: the last row of shapes in the table of Chapter 1, the snowflake sequence: five shapes that start from a triangle with equal sides and add smaller triangle bumps on every side
video_script.payoff_line: The first shape has three of each, and the later shapes have six of each

final_answer.value: Lines of symmetry: 3, 6, 6, 6, 6. Angles of symmetry: 3, 6, 6, 6, 6.
final_answer.spoken: the lines of symmetry are three, six, six, six and six, and the angles of symmetry are also three, six, six, six and six

never_show: a later snowflake shape shown with more than 6 fold lines
the full turn left out of a list of turns
maths_rules: first shape, a triangle with 3 equal sides: 3 lines of symmetry; turns 120, 240, 360 so 3 angles
second shape, a six pointed star: 6 lines (3 through opposite points, 3 through opposite notches); 360 / 6 = 60, turns 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 360 so 6 angles
third, fourth and fifth shapes: smaller bumps are added the same way on every side, so the same 6 lines and the same 6 turns work
lines of symmetry for the 5 shapes: 3, 6, 6, 6, 6
angles of symmetry for the 5 shapes: 3, 6, 6, 6, 6
slip: more bumps do not give more fold lines
video_script.design: One idea: bumps added the same way on every side keep the same fold lines and the same turns. Five shapes in a row, in the order of the book's table. Fold lines are teal and turns are amber.

<bookmark mark='row'/>It has five snowflake shapes. The first is a triangle, and each next shape grows smaller bumps.

narration: <bookmark mark='line'/>A fold line where both halves cover each other is called a line of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='angle'/>A turn about the centre that makes the shape look the same is called an angle of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='full'/>A full turn always fits, so it is counted as one of the angles.

<bookmark mark='turn'/>It fits after one hundred twenty, two hundred forty and three hundred sixty degrees.
<bookmark mark='write'/>It has three lines and three angles.

narration: <bookmark mark='star'/>Step two, the second shape is a star with six points.
<bookmark mark='fold'/>Three fold lines go through opposite points. Three more go through opposite notches between the points.
<bookmark mark='turn'/>Three hundred sixty divided by six is sixty. The star fits at every sixty degrees, up to the full turn.
<bookmark mark='write'/>It has six lines and six angles.

<bookmark mark='turn'/>Each of them also fits at every sixty degrees. More bumps do not add new lines or new turns.

<bookmark mark='all'/>For every shape, the lines equal the angles.
